author: Griffin Missant
title: Has ESPN's 'College GameDay' Gone Astray? - NewsBreak
text:
By Griffin Missant ,
21 hours ago USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect For decades, ESPN’s “College GameDay” was one of the defining traditions of college football Saturdays.
At times, the show was bigger than the games themselves, bringing fans together with memorable signs, campus traditions, expert analysis, and — of course — Lee Corso putting on a mascot head.
With “GameDay” about to celebrate its 40th anniversary in 2027, here’s a look at where the gold standard for pre-game shows stands now.
Get exclusive sports stories delivered to your inbox. Sign up for our newsletter today.
The Good News Sep 21, 2026; Inglewood, CA, USA; Pat McAfee on the ESPN Monday Night Countdown set at SoFi Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images The show finished the 2025-26 season with its best regular-season audience numbers ever, averaging 2.7 million viewers per episode. The Week 1 episode featuring Lee Corso’s retirement even had a whopping 4 million viewers. ESPN has also maintained a significant position over FOX’s “Big Noon Kickoff,” with over twice as many viewers.
Love him or hate him, people watch Pat McAfee. His own ESPN program had its most-watched year in 2025, averaging 436,000 viewers across TV and digital platforms. McAfee brings an audience and creates moments that spread well beyond the broadcast.
The show has even received praise from politicians, with Sen. Marco Rubio recently calling “College GameDay” the best show on all of television.
So what exactly is the problem?
Related: College Football’s Dumbest Losses of All Time
Sep 12, 2026; Austin, Texas, USA; Ted Cruz walks on field before the game between Ohio State Buckeyes and Texas Longhorns at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Scott Wachter-Imagn Images This season, an increasingly loud argument is that “College GameDay” has lost its luster.
The criticism has come from several directions.
First came the decision to give U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz nearly 10 minutes to discuss the Protect College Sports Act. The segment drew loud boos from the Texas crowd and sparked criticism over why a political discussion had such a prominent place on a college football pregame show.
Then there is the show’s location strategy. Early in the season, “GameDay” has focused solely on SEC campuses, going to Baton Rouge, Austin, Oxford and now Knoxville to start the 2026 season. The criticism is particularly notable because the show has historically prided itself on traveling to the biggest and most interesting college football environments, regardless of conference.
But now that the SEC’s media rights are exclusively with ABC/ESPN, the perception that there is an “SEC Bias” at The Worldwide Leader in Sports has only grown.
And then there is McAfee.
McAfee has undoubtedly changed “GameDay.” Some viewers love his energy, personality, and ability to turn a crowd into part of the show. Others believe the constant shouting, antics, and crowd interaction have pushed the actual college football discussion further into the background.
Recent criticism has argued that the McAfee Era has replaced some of the show’s traditional personality with a more entertainment-driven approach that favors style over substance.
Perhaps GameDay isn’t actually declining; maybe its audience is simply changing.
The show feels increasingly designed for the casual viewer who wants entertainment, celebrity appearances, big personalities and viral moments. Meanwhile, some longtime fans who fell in love with Corso, Kirk Herbstreit, and the show’s emphasis on the games themselves feel increasingly alienated.
Corso is irreplaceable, and McAfee was never destined to fill that role, given their different personalities. The real issue with College GameDay isn’t declining ratings but losing the soul that made those ratings matter in the first place. The numbers say the show’s metrics indicate success; longtime fans don’t share that sentiment.
